Md Harunur Rashid, Advocate — For the Petitioners. 
Chandi Charan Paul, Advocate — For the Opposite Party No. 14.
parties:
Amirunnessa & others ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Abdul Mannan and  others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Feeling aggrieved by an order passed by the learned District Judge in refusing to exercise inherent power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and maintaining the order of dismissal for default of a Miscellaneous case under Order 41 rule 19 of the Code of Civil Procedure arising out of an order of dismissal for default in a Title Appeal preferred against a Decree, the defendant-petitioners approached this Court in an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for quashing the order of dismissal whereupon a Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the order complained of in the petition moved in court should not be set aside. 

 6. The defendant-petitioners, against the said decree, carried an appeal being Title Appeal No. 115 of 1986 before the Court of District Judge, Pirojpur. The said appeal was dismissed for default on 18-5-1989. The petitioner, thereafter, filed an application being numbered as Miscellaneous Case No. 45 of 1989 under the provisions of Order 41 rule 19 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of the appeal. The said Miscellaneous Case was, also, dismissed for default on 9-9-89. Thereafter, the defendant-petitioners filed an application which was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 88 of 1989 under section 151 of the Code for restoration of the Miscellaneous case which was dismissed for default on 9-9-89 taking the stand that they were taking proper steps regularly in the appeal and the defendant-petitioner No. 1 having been an old lady was attacked with rheumatic fever and, as such, could not appear in the court on 9-9-89. The further stand taken was that in the family of the petitioners, there had not been any adult male person who could be sent to the learned Advocate on the date fixed for hearing and they sustained injury by the order of dismissal. 

 7. The learned District Judge dismissed the said case with the finding that the remedy by way of an appeal having been available to the petitioners, the application under section 151 of the Code was not at all maintainable. The learned District Judge, however, observed that the petitioners could prefer an appeal against the order of dismissal of the appeal. 

 12. Law is settled that a proceeding under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot be resorted to where there is alternative remedy available for seeking redress. The inherent power conferred under section 151 of the Code can be available in a case where there is no other provision for providing a redress. Power under section 151 of the Code can be invoked by a court only when the court is satisfied that prevention of the abuse of the process of the court is necessary or when ends of justice demand that the wrong complained of would be remedied. In the name of ends of justice, the remedy provided in the Code itself cannot be allowed to be negatived and also to be thwarted. The court, of course, under section 151 of the Code preserves the power to set aside order passed under misapprehension of facts when true facts are brought to light. The court also got the inherent power to vacate any order obtained by misleading the court and practising fraud upon it. The court, in the exercise of the power under section 151 of the Code, also, can correct the unintentional or inadvertent mistake committed by it. The court also preserves the inherent power to vacate any order if the same is passed under misapprehension of law. But the power cannot be invoked in cases which would result in overriding the express provision of law. 

 "Section 151 of the Civil Procedure Code does not formulate any new doctrine but is only a legislative recognition of the well-known principle that every Court has inherent power to act ex debito  justitiae and to do that real justice for the administration of which alone it exists. "Ends of justice" are solemn words and not mere polite expression in juristic methodology and here secreted in the solemn words is the aspiration that justice is the pursuit and end of all law. But the words "Ends of justice", wide as they are, do not, however, mean vague and indeterminate notions of justice, but justice according to the statutes and laws of the land. They cannot mean that express provisions of the statute can be overridden at the dictates of what, one might by private emotion or arbitrary preference call or conceive to be justice between the parties." Reference may be made to a decision in the case of Abdur Rahman Mizi and another vs. Abdul Wadud Mia, PLD 1953 Dhaka 83 = PLR Dhaka Series Vol II (7952) 287. Ibrahim, J after considering a large number of authorities of India held thus : 

 The case of Pujari Bhuj Das vs. Saiyeda Jobeda Begum 22 DLR Dhaka 383, Rajendra Shirah vs. Mahadev, 27 DLR 321, Azizur Rahman vs. Janata Bank, 28 DLR 252, Punjab Ali vs. Mokarram Hossain, 29 DLR 85 and Abdul Kader Chowdhury vs. Nurul Islam, 43 DLR (AD) 128 may be noticed in this regard. 

 15. Md Harunur Rashid refering to a decision in the case of Sarbeswar Mondal vs. Fakir Chand Sarker and others 14 DLR 256 contended that to secure the ends of justice the inherent power of the Code can be exercised under section 151 of the Code and the application under the said section cannot be thrown out in limine on the ground that an alternative remedy is available to him. In the cited case the question was whether an application under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code having been allowed ex parte, an application for setting aside the said Order 47, rule 1 read with section 151 of the said Code without moving High Court under section 115 of the Code is maintainable. In the said case it was held that it is not disputed that for ends of justice inherent power of the court can be exercised under section 151 of the Code whereas the scope of section 115 of the Code is more or less of a limited type and, as such, it is not a regular remedy which an aggrieved party can seek as a matter of right. Fact of the cited case is quite distinguishable in the facts and circumstances of the present case. The power exercised under section 115 of the Code is a discretionary one but the power exercised in appeal under Order 43 of the Code is a statutory one. The cited case, thus, is of no assistance to the petitioners. 

 16. Turning back to the merit of the present Rule it transpires from materials on record that appeal preferred by the defendant-petitioners was dismissed for default on 18-5-1989. The Miscellaneous Case under Order 41, rule 19 of the Code had been filed on 17-6-1989 and the same was also dismissed for default on 9-9-1989. Thereafter, the application under section 151 of the Code had been filed on 29-11-1989 that is after a period of 2 months and 20 days without any explanation of delay in filing the said application. It is significant to note here that the said application under section 151 of the Code had been signed only by Amirunnessa, the defendant-petitioner No. 1 out of the 5 defendant-petitioners and the said application had not been even signed by the learned Advocate, might be on the impression that he was not required to put signature on the said application as because he was the conducting lawyer for the petitioners both in the appeal as well as in the Miscellaneous Case under Order 41, rule 19 of the Code, although, the learned Advocate argued the case before the court of learned District Judge in support of the petition under section 151 of the Code. The order of dismissal dated 9-9-1989, though was appealable order no appeal had been preferred. The defendant-petitioners instead of availing the said remedy of appeal filed an application under section 151 of the Code which was not at all permitted by law. There is, also no allegation that the order under challenge was the result of a mistake of a court or the same was passed under a misapprehension of law or a fraud had been practised upon the court in obtaining the order. The learned District Judge in the order under challenge observed that the petitioner could prefer appeal against the order of dismissal passed in the Miscellaneous case under Order 41, rule 19 of the Code. The fruitless proceeding under section 151 of the Code did not deter the petitioners from moving this Court in Revisional application under section 115 of the Code. 

 18. Before parting with the case I feel inclined to observe that a lawyer engaged by a litigant public has no right to absent himself from a court when the case of his client comes up for hearing. It is the bounden duty on the part of the learned lawyer to attend to that case in the court or he can make such other arrangement for the proper representation of the case of his client in the court. The learned lawyer owes a duty not only to his client but also to the court. In this particular case the learned lawyer though engaged by the petitioners both in the appeal as well as in the Miscellaneous case under Order 41, rule 19 of the Code, did not present himself in the court to represent the case of his clients, that is, the petitioners before me. I also feel observing that the proceeding under section 151 of the Code before the court of District Judge and the Revision Petition before this Court is a flagrant misuse of the mercies of law, the same having no survival value. The party concerned, here the petitioners, appear  to have prevailed upon the learned lawyer to present to this court a case which is wholly misconceived. The petitioners could be advised by the learned Lawyer to prefer appeal under Order 43 of the Code against the said order of dismissal of the said Miscellaneous case as observed by the learned District Judge in the said case. A learned lawyer owes a sacred duty to the society not to encourage shady cases by which courts might be overburdened denying justice to the genuine litigants. The learned members of the Bar as the officers of the court and also as the companion of the cause of justice may have valuable contribution to the cause of justice if they screen out frivolous and fraudulent litigations and refuse to accept them saving the courts from being over-flooded with frivolous, fraudulent and misconceived cases. It is expected that the co-operation of the Bar will be readily forthcoming in this regard.
